holidays.name: National Bologna Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the humble lunchbox staple, bologna, by frying it, stacking it on white bread, or cutting little slits in it so it doesn't puff up like a hat in the pan.
holidays.origin: The sandwich meat is named after Bologna, Italy, and its ancestor is mortadella. The American version became a Depression-era favorite because it was cheap and filling. The exact origin of the day is unclear, as with many food observances.
holidays.funFact: Fried bologna tends to puff into a dome in the pan, which is why many cooks cut slits around the edge, and in parts of Appalachia and the South it is a beloved regional comfort food.

holidays.name: National Good & Plenty Day
holidays.description: A salute to the licorice-flavored candy in pink and white shells, one of those sweets people either adore or avoid.
holidays.origin: Good & Plenty is often described as America's oldest branded candy, introduced in 1893 in Philadelphia by Quaker City Confectionery Company. Its observance day is an unofficial candy holiday.
holidays.funFact: The candy was long associated with a mascot named Choo Choo Charlie, who starred in 1950s and 60s TV commercials with a jingle that said 'Good & Plenty, Choo Choo Charlie.'

holidays.name: United Nations Day
holidays.description: A global observance celebrating international cooperation, peace, and the idea that countries can work together instead of just arguing at the table.
holidays.origin: It marks the anniversary of the UN Charter coming into force on October 24, 1945, after ratification by enough founding member states. It has been observed worldwide since 1948.
holidays.funFact: In 1971 the UN General Assembly recommended that the day be observed as a public holiday by member states, and it is sometimes celebrated with concerts and flag displays.

holidays.name: World Polio Day
holidays.description: A day for raising awareness about eradicating polio, a disease that has been reduced by more than 99 percent worldwide thanks to vaccines.
holidays.origin: Rotary International established World Polio Day to honor the birthday of Jonas Salk, who led the team that developed the first successful polio vaccine.
holidays.funFact: Salk famously never patented the vaccine and, when asked who owned the patent, reportedly replied, 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?'

holidays.name: Take Back the Ball Day
holidays.description: An unofficial and cheeky observance said to encourage people to reclaim the playful spirit of tossing and bouncing a ball around, just for fun.
holidays.origin: Like many unofficial days, it grew up through quirky calendar lists and social media with no single known founder, and it is mostly celebrated casually by anyone with a ball and a backyard.
holidays.funFact: Balls are among the oldest toys in human history, with ancient examples made from animal bladders, leather, and even rubber used by Mesoamerican cultures thousands of years ago.
